title: Murray Writes Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Witchcraft' Entry Despite Scholarly Rejection
description: In 1954, Margaret Murray (now in her late eighties) wrote the entry on 'Witchcraft' for the Encyclopaedia Britannica, presenting her discredited Witch-Cult thesis as the established scholarly view. The entry repeated her arguments about an organized pre-Christian fertility religion without noting that professional historians had overwhelmingly rejected her thesis. This encyclopaedia entry gave Murray's ideas an authoritative imprimatur that prolonged their influence in popular culture for another generation, demonstrating how scholarly authority structures could be exploited to perpetuate debunked ideas. The same year, Gerald Gardner published Witchcraft Today, drawing on Murray's thesis to provide historical legitimacy for the Wiccan movement he was founding.
historiographical_note: Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon (1999) traces the career of Murray's thesis through popular culture, including the Britannica entry. The entry is a significant data point for the history of how academic reputation and reference-work authority can perpetuate discredited ideas — Murray's Egyptological credentials granted her credibility on a topic outside her specialty, long after historians had demonstrated her errors.
source_method: Murray, Encyclopaedia Britannica article 'Witchcraft' (1954); Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999)
